grounds.point: M.L. Sharma occupied part of 40/16 under an employment-linked permission and remained there after his employment had ended.
grounds.explanation: Respondents 2-4 pleaded that M.L. Sharma received the accommodation through his employment and continued residing there after retirement; RW2 also described him as an employee permitted to reside there, while RW3 stated that he was no longer employed in 1998-1999 and died at 40/16. These are pleadings and evidence rather than a supplied final court finding, and physical occupation alone does not establish the statutory character of subletting, assignment or parting with possession.

grounds.point: National Insurance sublet, assigned or otherwise parted with possession of the relevant portion to M.L. Sharma, Roop Sharma or Rajiv Nanda.
grounds.explanation: The petitioner alleged exclusive possession and statutory subletting or parting, while respondent No.1 denied any such transfer and respondents 2-4 characterized M.L. Sharma's occupation as employment accommodation and Roop Sharma and Rajiv Nanda as visiting relatives. The reported Parasaram passage confirms that Delhi section 14(b) is broad enough to encompass sublease, assignment and other modes of parting with possession, but the supplied law does not decide when employment-linked accommodation followed by continued post-employment residence becomes one of those categories; the withheld final reasoning cannot be supplied by inference.

grounds.point: Any qualifying subletting, assignment or parting with possession occurred on or after 9 June 1952.
grounds.explanation: The record places M.L. Sharma's employment in 1952, describes his permitted use as existing before 1972, and supplies evidence of residence long afterward, but it gives no definite date on which a legally qualifying transfer or parting occurred. Because the supplied law does not establish that continued residence after retirement itself constitutes a new or continuing statutory parting, the clause's temporal premise cannot be conclusively applied.

grounds.point: The alleged subletting, assignment or parting with possession was without the landlord's consent in writing.
grounds.explanation: The petitioner expressly alleged absence of written consent, while respondents 2-4 denied that the portion had been given to them without such consent; no actual written consent concerning the alleged occupation is identified in the supplied record. Section 14(1)(b) makes absence of written landlord consent material, and section 17 likewise refers to previous written consent for post-Act subletting, but no supplied burden rule permits the competing pleadings or the absence of a produced document to be upgraded into a finding.

grounds.point: An involuntary, statutory or court-effected transfer is categorically exempt from Delhi Rent Control Act section 14(1)(b).
grounds.explanation: The supplied Supreme Court report of Parasaram states that the amplitude of Delhi section 14(b) extends even to an involuntary sale, so involuntariness alone is not a categorical exemption. Telesound expressed only a prima facie view concerning amalgamation and expressly reserved the section 14(1)(b) eviction question, while General Radio's adopted application concerned a different Andhra Pradesh statute; these authorities therefore do not establish that the New Zealand Insurance-to-National Insurance vesting either proves or defeats this eviction ground.

reason: The supplied record supports long-term occupation by M.L. Sharma and defeats any categorical claim that an involuntary transfer is automatically outside section 14(1)(b), but it does not resolve whether National Insurance legally sublet, assigned or parted with possession, when any qualifying event occurred, or whether it occurred without written landlord consent. Those unresolved statutory premises prevent the fixed eviction ground from being established or refuted on the allowed material alone.
